A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RTD research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval experiments, component ablations, backbone comparisons, and supplementary GeneCIS, COCO, and noise-sensitivity results.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds evaluated integrations, training-data comparisons, dataset-size experiments, and filtering ablations.

M1.justification: The core loss, anchoring, batch sampling, and noisy concatenation remain unchanged. Appendix A.3 adds adaptations: FTI4CIR omits its attribute projector during RTD training and supplies attributes textually, while Context-I2W receives a text encoder trained with Pic2Word's projector. A LLaMA3 in-context triplet-generation option is also introduced.

E1.justification: The five evaluation benchmarks remain unchanged, including GeneCIS and COCO already present in v1. Training coverage expands beyond CompoDiff and CC3M template triplets to include IP2P, WebVid2M-derived CoVR, VQA2.0-derived CASE, and CC3M in-context triplets (Table 6; Appendix A.2). This substantially broadens training sources, including video-caption and VQA-derived data.

E2.justification: v1's main comparisons cover Pic2Word, SEARLE, and LinCIR. v2 Table 2 adds Context-I2W and FTI4CIR with and without RTD, plus KEDs, CIReVL, LDRE, MT-CIR, MagicLens, CompoDiff, CoVR, and CASE. Table 4 also adds a pair-update comparator to the corresponding text-to-image experiment.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark splits, retrieval metrics, and default optimization settings are retained. New experimental designs introduce FSC-CLIP, training subsets of 1K, 50K, and 100K triplets, mixtures reported up to 5.05M, and filtered versus unfiltered training controls (Tables 2 and 17–19). ViT-G/14 was already evaluated in v1.

E4.justification: Beyond retained component, noise, and partial-layer ablations, v2 adds a pair-update control to the discrepancy test, expands the triplet-source analysis, and investigates training-data scale and filtering dependence (Table 4, Table 6, Appendices B.5–B.6). These provide substantial new evidence about attribution, data efficiency, and robustness to training-data construction.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. References to Gaussian standard deviation concern injected training noise, not uncertainty in reported results.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark, efficient-variant, and noise-ablation tables retain their numerical values after relocation. v2 adds substantial results for new integrations, comparators, training sources, scaling, filtering, and runtime. For example, Table 4 newly reports pair-update mAP@10 of 11.15 alongside the retained frozen-encoder 10.71 and RTD 15.80.

T1.justification: Equation (1), the embedding definitions, and the target-anchoring assumption retain their mathematical content. The equation is reformatted; no new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: v1 primarily claims improved projection-based zero-shot CIR through efficient text-only training. v2 makes competitiveness with resource-intensive synthetic-triplet methods a central claim, including comparable or superior performance with 23 minutes of additional training and claimed training speedups up to 100×. This comparative contribution now anchors the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for CASE's weak results, small-data sufficiency, and transfer between projection modules. It acknowledges unequal comparison settings and potential CASE/COCO overlap. Appendix E introduces specific limits on applicability beyond projection-based CIR, replacing v1's benchmark-noise-focused limitations discussion, although some dataset-noise warnings remain in Appendix A.1.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 substantially expands documentation of source corpora, LLMs, generation strategies, and triplet counts; Appendix A.3 explains the new integrations. Training iterations, runtime, hardware, and generation costs are added in Section 3, Table 1, and Appendix C. v2 also adds code-release and reproducibility statements, whose actual code availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: The paper shifts from explicitly excluding resource-intensive CIR methods from comparison to positioning RTD against them on performance and efficiency. Related work expands to newer projection methods, training-free approaches, and composition-tuned backbones, including FTI4CIR, Context-I2W, LDRE, FashionERN, and FSC-CLIP.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and related-work narrative are substantially revised. The discrepancy analysis moves from Section 3.3 to Section 4.4, analyses are reorganized into separate subsections, and efficient-update results move to Appendix B.4. The supplement gains expanded implementation, limitations, and reproducibility sections.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one-column to two-column layout. v2 redraws Figure 2, adds the backbone-summary Figure 3, and introduces a consolidated comparison Table 2. Existing detailed results move to the supplement, while runtime, training-source, scaling, and filtering tables are added. Existing qualitative examples are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: Broader comparisons, additional controls, data-scale/filtering experiments, and integration details improve the evidential basis and reproducibility beyond v1. The gain is limited by new reporting inconsistencies: Table 6 reports CoVR/CASE averages of 41.9/37.7, although its listed metrics average approximately 40.9/37.3. Section 4.2 also claims standard CLIP-L/14 LinCIR+RTD outperforms MagicLens on FashionIQ, contrary to Table 2. These errors weaken the strengthened conclusions.
